en: God, bless the Hungarian
With good cheer, with plenty,
Stretch out a protecting arm towards him
When he fights with the enemy;
Him whom ill fate has long been tearing,
Bring upon him a merry year,
This people has already atoned
For the past and the future!
Our ancestors you brought up
Onto the holy peaks of the Carpathians,
Through you a fair homeland was won
By the blood of Bendegúz.
And wherever the waves roar
Of the Tisza, of the Danube,
Árpád's heroic offspring
Burst into flower.
For us on the fields of Kumania
You waved the ripe ears of grain,
On the vine shoots of Tokaj
You dripped nectar.
Our flag you often planted
On the wild Turk's ramparts,
And under Matthias's grim army groaned
Vienna's proud castle.
Alas, but because of our sins
Anger kindled in your breast,
And you struck down your lightnings
From your thundering cloud,
Now the plundering Mongol's arrows
You sent whirring above us,
Then from the Turk a slave's yoke
We took upon our shoulders.
How often there sounded on the lips
Of Osman's wild people,
Over the bone heaps of our beaten army,
A song of victory!
How often your own son rose
Against your breast, my fair homeland,
And you became, because of your offspring,
The urn of your offspring's ashes!
The persecuted one hid, and towards him
A sword reaches into his cave,
He looked all around and did not find
His home in the homeland,
He climbs to the peak and goes down to the valley,
Grief and doubt beside him,
A flood of blood at his feet,
And a sea of flame above him.
A castle stood, now a heap of stones,
Gladness and joy flitted about,
The rattle of death, lamentation
Now surge in their place.
And ah, freedom does not bloom
From the blood of the dead,
Tears of tormenting slavery fall
From the burning eyes of orphans!
Have pity, God, on the Hungarian
Whom storms of peril have tossed,
Stretch out a protecting arm towards him
On the sea of his torment.
Him whom ill fate has long been tearing,
Bring upon him a merry year,
This people has already atoned
For the past and the future!
notes: The poem addresses God throughout; 'you' and 'your' are God, except in stanza 5, lines 5-8, which turn to the homeland.
line 2.4: Bendegúz is the legendary father of Attila, whom Hungarian tradition took as an ancestor.
line 2.7: Árpád led the Hungarians into the Carpathian Basin (c. 895).
line 3.1: Kunság (Cumania) is the plain between the Danube and the Tisza settled by the Cumans.
line 3.7: Mátyás is King Matthias Corvinus, who took Vienna in 1485; 'bús' usually means 'sad', here grim or fierce [?].
line 5.2: 'Ozmán' is Osman, founder of the Ottoman dynasty; his people are the Ottoman Turks.
line 5.5: 'tennfiad' (your own son) refers to Hungarians who fought against Hungarians.
